chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Isma'il ibn Ja'far, who said:

Two men disputed before Dawud (peace be upon him) regarding a cow. This one brought evidence that it was his, and that one brought evidence that it was his. He said: So Dawud (peace be upon him) entered the mihrab (prayer niche/place of worship) and said: 'O Lord, judging between these two has overwhelmed me, so You be the One who judges.' Then God, Exalted and Glorious, revealed to him: 'Go out, take the cow from the one who has it in his hand, give it to the other, and strike his neck.'

He said: So the Children of Israel murmured against that, saying: 'This one brought evidence and that one brought evidence, and the one more entitled to be given it is the one who has it in his hands.' So he took it from him, struck his neck, and gave it to this one.

He said: So Dawud (peace be upon him) entered the mihrab and said: 'O Lord, the Children of Israel have murmured against what You judged.' So his Lord revealed to him: 'The one who had the cow in his hand had met the father of the other and killed him, and took the cow from him. So when a similar case comes to you, judge between them according to what you see, and do not ask Me to judge until the Reckoning.'

key_terms.الْحِسَابُ: The Reckoning, accounting in the Hereafter
key_terms.الْمِحْرَابُ: Mihrab, prayer niche or place of worship
key_terms.دَاوُدُ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: Dawud (peace be upon him), Prophet David

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Dawud (AS) and the disputed cow in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the concept of *al-hukm bi-z-zahir* (judging by appearances) versus *al-hukm bi-l-batin* (judging by inner truth), a key distinction in Shia jurisprudence. It highlights Prophet Dawud’s (AS) use of divine inspiration (*wahy*) to discern the hidden reality of the dispute—specifically that the current holder had killed the claimant's father—thereby justifying his seemingly arbitrary ruling to the Israelites. The narrative underscores the Prophet's role as a judge who relies on God's guidance to resolve ambiguities that human evidence alone cannot fully clarify.
